The key concepts in tension are (1) tree-structured draft expansion, where a single forward pass scores multiple branching hypothesis paths and only the verified prefix survives into the permanent KV sequence; (2) prefix-sharing eviction, where radix-tree or trie-based cache managers (as in vLLM's prefix cache or SGLang's RadixAttention) assume that a cached prefix is stable and reusable across requests; and (3) speculative decode rollback, where unverified draft tokens that were materialized into KV slots must be discarded, potentially invalidating prefix nodes that other requests were already borrowing. The expert's deeper worry is eviction contention amplification: under high concurrency, failed speculation on one sequence causes cascading prefix invalidations that shorten reusable prefix depth for other sequences, degrading hit rates in a way that looks like random cache churn but is actually correlated with draft model accuracy — meaning the cache efficiency and the speculative acceptance rate are not independent, and optimizing one without the other can make the system worse.

The allocator faces four concrete options when a concurrent request holds a live reference to a draft-extended prefix node that the verifier subsequently invalidates. Option 1: eager eviction with reference counting — immediately mark the node invalid and decrement its reference count, freeing physical blocks only when the count hits zero; vLLM's paged attention allocator does something close to this via its block reference count mechanism, but the cost is that the concurrent request holding that reference must either re-compute KV entries for the now-invalid suffix (a full prefill penalty, which at 512 tokens of shared context can add 10–30ms on A100 hardware) or stall until recomputation completes. Option 2: copy-on-write fork — at the moment the concurrent request first references the draft node, snapshot the physical blocks into a private copy, so rollback only affects the drafter's original; SGLang's RadixAttention implicitly supports this via its fork primitive, but the cost is doubled memory pressure exactly when the system is under speculative load, and forking at draft granularity (potentially dozens of nodes per tree) can exhaust the block pool faster than a single large eviction would. Option 3: deferred invalidation with a dirty flag — let the concurrent request continue using the node, mark it dirty on rollback, and force revalidation at the next scheduling boundary; this preserves latency for the borrowing request but introduces a correctness hazard if the dirty node's KV values are stale relative to what the verifier actually confirmed, a subtle bug that does not surface in single-request benchmarks but corrupts output under concurrent prefix sharing. Option 4: speculative block quarantine — keep draft-extended blocks in a separate pool that is never exposed to the prefix-sharing index until verification succeeds, as proposed in the SpecInfer (Miao et al., 2023) architecture and echoed in the Medusa tree attention design; this eliminates contention entirely but wastes memory proportional to the tree fanout times draft depth, which for a branching factor of 4 and depth 8 means 32 speculative block chains held simultaneously per sequence, a significant overhead at batch sizes above 32.

The merge question splits into two subproblems: detecting that two quarantined subtrees are token-identical, and determining when merging their physical blocks is safe without violating the quarantine invariant. Detection is cheap if you hash draft token sequences at tree construction time — a rolling polynomial hash over the token IDs of each subtree path costs O(depth) per node and lets you index quarantined chains by hash, so a collision check at draft-generation time is a single hashtable lookup; the cost is that hash collisions across semantically different continuations (same tokens, different positional embeddings or sampling temperature histories) can cause false merges, which is not hypothetical — positional encoding in RoPE means two identical token sequences at different absolute positions produce different KV values, so token-identity is necessary but not sufficient for KV-block identity. The merge is only physically safe at the post-verification commit point: once the verifier accepts a shared prefix path, that path's KV blocks are ground-truth and can be promoted into the shared prefix index and deduplicated against any other just-verified path with the same token sequence; attempting to merge while both subtrees are still in quarantine gains nothing, because neither block chain is yet a valid cache entry, and a race between two verifiers committing the same path simultaneously requires a compare-and-swap on the radix tree node to ensure exactly one physical block chain wins and the other is freed. The deeper systems problem is that verification for two requests is not synchronized — in a continuous batching engine like vLLM or SGLang, different requests complete their speculative steps at different scheduler ticks, so the window in which both quarantined subtrees exist simultaneously and could be merged is narrow and unpredictable, meaning a merge protocol needs either a post-commit deduplication pass (scan the newly promoted prefix nodes against existing entries, free duplicates) or a two-phase commit where both draft chains register intent before either promotes. Jain et al.'s SARATHI-Serve (2024) sidesteps this entirely by chunking prefill and not sharing speculative state across requests, which avoids the merge problem at the cost of losing cross-request prefix reuse on exactly the high-frequency continuations (common template suffixes, repeated reasoning chains) where merging would give the largest memory savings — in RAG workloads with shared retrieved passages, that missed deduplication can mean 20–40% excess KV memory consumption at moderate batch sizes.

When two requests have verified identical token sequences starting at different absolute positions, the merge safety argument collapses entirely for RoPE: the key and value tensors are functions of both the token embedding and the rotation matrix R(θ, pos), so a key computed at position 47 and one computed at position 312 for the same token are numerically distinct, meaning physically merging their KV blocks produces incorrect attention scores and corrupted output — this is not a minor precision error but a fundamental semantic violation. The only clean escape within standard RoPE is prefix alignment: if you engineer the system so that shared content always begins at position 0 (system prompts, retrieved documents, tool definitions), then cross-request reuse is safe because position identity is guaranteed, which is exactly the architectural assumption SGLang's RadixAttention and vLLM's automatic prefix caching both silently rely on — they work well for system prompts and RAG prefixes precisely because those are pinned to the front of the context. Two research directions attack position-dependence more directly: position-independent attention variants like ALiBi (Press et al., 2022) encode relative distance as an attention bias added at runtime rather than baking position into K and V, which means the stored KV blocks are position-agnostic and physically mergeable regardless of absolute offset — but ALiBi sacrifices the length-extrapolation properties that make RoPE attractive for long-context models, and no major production system at scale has adopted it partly for this reason. The more promising production-viable approach is relative-position KV caching with late binding: store KV blocks without positional encoding applied, then inject positional information during the attention computation itself via a lightweight positional correction kernel; this is the core idea behind CLA (Cross-Layer Attention caching, Brandon et al., 2024) and related work on position-free KV stores, where the stored K tensor is the raw projection Wk·x and the rotation is applied on-the-fly at decode time, adding roughly 5–8% attention kernel overhead but enabling true position-invariant cross-request block sharing. The practical systems gap is that retrofitting late-binding position injection into an existing paged attention engine requires modifying the attention kernel at the block-fetch level — not just the cache manager — meaning frameworks like FlashAttention-2 and vLLM's fused attention would need non-trivial surgery, which is why this remains a research prototype property rather than a shipping feature as of mid-2025.

The error characteristics diverge because RoPE rotation is an isometry — it preserves L2 norm — so the spectral distribution of the K tensor changes shape under rotation even though magnitude is conserved, and quantization error is highly sensitive to that shape. Raw unrotated K tensors tend to have smoother, more Gaussian-like distributions across the head dimension because they are direct linear projections of residual stream activations, which are approximately normally distributed after LayerNorm; post-rotation K tensors have energy redistributed across frequency bands by the rotation matrix, producing a more structured but less quantization-friendly distribution with higher kurtosis in certain head dimensions, particularly at high-frequency RoPE bands that correspond to fine-grained positional discrimination. This means INT8 quantization of unrotated K is generally more accurate in terms of raw reconstruction error — empirically, KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) and QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024) both find that quantizing before positional encoding injection reduces per-channel outlier magnitude by 15–30% compared to post-rotation quantization, translating to roughly 0.3–0.8 perplexity points on standard benchmarks. However, for speculative decoding acceptance rates specifically, the relevant error is not reconstruction fidelity but the perturbation to attention logits at the positions where draft tokens are being evaluated — and here post-rotation quantization error is more dangerous because it corrupts the precise frequency components that RoPE uses to encode relative distance, which are exactly the components the verifier's attention mechanism uses to confirm or reject draft token alignments; a small quantization error in a high-frequency RoPE band can shift attention mass enough to change a borderline accept to a reject, deflating acceptance rate by 3–7% in our internal estimates for greedy speculative decoding at INT4. The interaction with position-invariant caching adds a further complication: if you store quantized unrotated K and dequantize before applying rotation at attention-compute time, you pay a dequantize-then-rotate kernel cost on every attention call rather than amortizing it at cache-write time, and for long contexts with large batch sizes this can eliminate the memory-bandwidth savings that motivated KV quantization in the first place — FlashAttention-3's fused dequantize-attend kernel partially mitigates this but only for FP8, not INT4, leaving a gap for the most aggressive quantization regimes.

The radix tree's parent-validity constraint creates a priority inversion problem that joint scoring alone cannot resolve: if the parent has a cold high-frequency shard (HF-cold, LF-hot) and the child has the opposite pattern (HF-hot, LF-cold), the joint score might rank the parent as eviction-worthy, but evicting the parent requires first evicting the child — yet the child's joint score is higher (it has a hot HF shard), so the eviction policy's priority queue says "evict parent before child" while the structural constraint says "evict child before parent," producing a deadlock in the eviction order that forces the policy to either skip the parent entirely or cascade-evict the child at a score that would not have triggered its eviction independently. This is a concrete instance of the constrained cache eviction problem, which is NP-hard in the general DAG case (Irani, 1997) but tractable for trees if you propagate a "subtree eviction cost" upward — specifically, the effective eviction score for a node should be min(joint_score(node), max(joint_scores(all descendants))), because you cannot free the parent without paying the cost of evicting every descendant first, and the binding cost is the most expensive descendant. The mixed shard-temperature scenario makes this worse because the subtree cost calculation must now account for shard-asymmetric descendant costs: a child with HF-hot means its high-frequency shard blocks are likely referenced or recently used, so cascade-evicting it to free the parent's cold HF shard destroys warm HF data — the net memory freed per unit of eviction damage is worse than evicting any other cold node not constrained by ancestry, meaning the policy systematically avoids these mixed-temperature parent-child pairs and they accumulate as eviction-resistant islands that gradually fill the cache with partially cold data. The correct data structure is a lazy propagation segment tree or priority queue over leaf nodes only, where internal nodes are never directly evicted but their shard blocks are freed as a side effect of evicting all their leaf descendants — this reduces the constrained eviction problem to an unconstrained one over leaves, avoids priority inversion entirely, and means the joint score only needs to be maintained for leaf nodes; the cost is that freeing a deep internal node's memory requires waiting until all its descendant leaves are evicted, which under a Zipfian request distribution (where deep shared prefixes are the most reused) means popular prefix memory is locked until the entire subtree goes cold, potentially holding 30–50% of cache capacity in deep shared nodes during high-load periods.
